title: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
name: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
description: A non-parametric, instance-based lazy learning algorithm that predicts using similarity to neighboring training samples.

decisionsummary.summary: KNN is a non-parametric, instance-based lazy learning algorithm that predicts by finding the k most similar training examples (under a chosen distance metric) and aggregating their labels or target values at query time.
bestusecases: Small to moderate sized tabular datasets where storage of training examples is acceptable and feature dimensionality is modest.
Low-latency prototyping and baseline models for classification/regression when interpretability via nearest examples is valuable.
Similarity-based recommendation or anomaly detection where nearest-neighbor retrieval maps naturally to business logic.
Problems where a simple local decision rule (neighbor voting or averaging) and inspection of nearest examples support audits and debugging.
avoidwhen: Very large training sets that cannot fit into memory or where real-time queries must be extremely fast without approximate indices.
High-dimensional sparse data (text TF-IDF, very wide feature vectors) where distance metrics degrade (curse of dimensionality).
Strict real-time, low-latency production systems without approximate neighbor indices or specialized hardware.
Memory-constrained deployments where storing all training instances is infeasible.
strengths: Conceptual and practical simplicity: training is trivial (store X,y) and predictions are explainable by showing nearest examples.
Flexible non-parametric behavior that adapts to arbitrary decision boundaries given sufficient local data density.
Minimal training compute; suitability for rapid iteration and easy incremental dataset updates (add/remove examples).
Works with arbitrary target types (classification voting, regression averaging) and supports distance-weighted predictions.
limitations: Query-time cost and memory usage scale with dataset size; naive prediction requires scanning many samples.
Performance collapses in high-dimensional spaces unless dimensionality reduction or feature selection is applied.
Sensitive to feature scaling, irrelevant features, and noise/outliers that distort distance calculations.
No explicit model generalization—no internal compact parameterization—so performance depends directly on training set coverage.
decisionsummary.interpretability: Neighbor-based prediction: each prediction can be justified by listing nearest training examples and their distances. Local decision regions: model induces Voronoi-like regions (for uniform weights) making the decision boundary intuitive. Distance-based reasoning: importance is explicit via distance metric and optional weighting (closer neighbors count more). Explainability through nearest examples supports audits—inspect example-level evidence rather than opaque parameters.
decisionsummary.trainingcharacteristics: Lazy learning: there is no parameter fitting step beyond storing training data and optionally building an index. No explicit model fitting required; 'training' time is dominated by optional index construction (KD-Tree, Ball-Tree) if used. Storage behavior: full training set (feature vectors + labels) must be retained for inference. Index construction: KD-Tree and Ball-Tree accelerate neighbor search for moderate dimensions; brute-force or approximate indices used otherwise.
decisionsummary.inferencecharacteristics: Neighbor search cost dominates: query executes nearest-neighbor search (exact or approximate), then aggregation. Latency per query depends on dataset size, search algorithm, and feature dimensionality—can be high without indexing. Distance computations are CPU-bound and memory-access heavy; throughput depends on cache locality and vectorized routines. Batch prediction can amortize costs but still requires neighbor retrieval for each query.
decisionsummary.computationalcharacteristics: Training complexity: O(1) nominal (store data) or O(n log n)–O(n) for index construction depending on index type and implementation. Prediction complexity (exact brute-force): O(n p) per query where n = samples, p = features. Neighbor search (KD-Tree/Ball-Tree): average O(log n) per query for low p but degrades with p; worst-case can be O(n). Memory usage: O(n p) to store dataset plus index overhead (O(n) to O(n log n) depending on index). Scalability limits: practical for n up to a few hundred thousand with approximate indices; impractical at very large scale without specialized ANN systems.

coreunderstanding.intuition: Similar instances have similar outputs; prediction is based on local neighborhoods rather than a global model. For classification, the class is typically the majority among k nearest neighbors (optionally distance-weighted). For regression, prediction is typically the average (or weighted average) of neighbor target values. Learning is lazy: no parametric fit; all computation moves to the query phase, making updates trivial (append/remove).
coreunderstanding.learningmechanism: Prediction is based on finding the k nearest neighbors in the feature space. The class or value of the query point is determined by aggregating the properties of these neighbors. Minkowski distance metrics are used to define closeness, and voting or averaging computes the final estimate. It is lazy learning: no parameters are optimized during training.
assumptions: Local smoothness: nearby points have similar labels/targets; violating this causes poor local predictions.
Meaningful distance metric: chosen metric reflects problem similarity; wrong metrics lead to irrelevant neighbors.
Proper feature scaling: features must be comparable; without scaling one feature can dominate distances.
Representative neighborhood: training set density must cover regions where queries occur; sparse regions yield unreliable neighbors.
Sufficient training density: if training density is low relative to required decision complexity, KNN underperforms.
coreunderstanding.mathematicalintuition: Single deep trees overfit; in contrast, KNN's prediction boundary is determined by local density. Small k (e.g. k=1) fits the noise in individual samples (low bias, high variance). Larger k averages over a wider local neighborhood, smoothing the decision boundary and reducing variance at the cost of increasing bias. Minkowski distance acts as the metric space framework.
coreunderstanding.complexity: O(n p) for brute-force prediction, O(k log n p) on average using trees for low-dimensional p.
coreunderstanding.memorycomplexity: O(n p) to store the raw training vectors and labels, plus tree index overhead of O(n) to O(n log n).
coreunderstanding.robustness: Moderate to monotonic transforms and small changes in data distribution (if k chosen appropriately). Not robust to label noise or heavy outliers.
coreunderstanding.scalability: Scales poorly with n and p for exact brute-force search; approximate nearest neighbor libraries (FAISS, Annoy, HNSW) extend scale to millions of vectors with trade-offs in exactness/latency.
coreunderstanding.overfittingtendency: Small k (e.g., k=1) leads to low bias and high variance (overfit to noise); larger k smooths predictions and reduces variance.
coreunderstanding.biasvariance: K controls bias-variance: increasing k increases bias and reduces variance; choosing k is a trade-off tuned via validation.

hyperparameters.name: n_neighbors
hyperparameters.purpose: Number of nearest neighbors used to make a prediction.
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Bias increases (smoother decision surface); variance decreases.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Accuracy vs stability: larger k stabilizes predictions but can blur local structure.
interactions: Interacts with feature scaling and metric choice; large k mitigates noisy metrics.
commonmistakes: Using odd k only for binary imbalance considerations but ignoring cross-validation; picking k larger than minority class count which biases results.

hyperparameters.name: weights
hyperparameters.purpose: How neighbor votes are weighted: 'uniform' (equal) or 'distance' (closer neighbors weighted more) or callable.
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Bias decreases for strong local signals; variance increases if weights amplify noise in few neighbors.
hyperparameters.decreaseeffect: Bias increases if local structure matters; variance decreases (towards uniform).
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Distance weighting can improve predictions where distance correlates strongly with label similarity, but it amplifies the effect of noisy close neighbors.
interactions: Interacts with metric and k selection.
commonmistakes: Applying distance weighting without stabilizing distances via scaling, leading to predictions dominated by a single feature difference.

hyperparameters.name: algorithm
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Bias/variance is unchanged (affects only computation), but approximate algorithms may introduce approximation error. Query speed increases for low-dimensional problems using tree structures.
hyperparameters.decreaseeffect: Query speed decreases for large dataset sizes.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Exactness vs speed: brute-force yields exact results but is slower; tree indices speed up queries for low-dimensional data; approximate ANN trades exactness for speed.
interactions: Interacts with leaf_size and metric choice. KD-Tree works best for low-dimensional Euclidean data.
commonmistakes: Using tree indices for very high-dimensional data where they provide no benefit and increase computational overhead.

hyperparameters.name: leaf_size
hyperparameters.purpose: Leaf size passed to tree-based algorithms affecting tree construction and query speed.
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: No effect on bias/variance. May speed up queries up to a point; very large leaves approach brute-force. Tree size shrinks.
hyperparameters.decreaseeffect: Can increase tree depth and query overhead. Tree structure may be larger.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Query latency vs tree index construction time.
commonmistakes: Over-optimizing leaf_size before profiling actual query latency in production.

hyperparameters.name: metric
hyperparameters.purpose: Distance metric used for neighbor comparisons (e.g., 'minkowski', 'euclidean', 'manhattan', custom).
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Can reduce bias if metric matches problem geometry, but can increase variance if metric overfits small structures. Custom or complex metrics are slower to compute.
hyperparameters.decreaseeffect: Simpler metrics compute faster but may increase bias if the metric mismatches data geometry.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Choosing a metric closest to domain similarity is critical; wrong metric dramatically reduces neighbor relevance.
interactions: Interacts with p (Minkowski parameter), metric_params, and feature scaling.
commonmistakes: Leaving metric=euclidean with unscaled heterogeneous features.

hyperparameters.name: p
hyperparameters.purpose: Power parameter for the Minkowski metric (p=1 Manhattan, p=2 Euclidean).
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Distance geometry changes: larger p emphasizes large coordinate differences, altering neighbor sets.
hyperparameters.decreaseeffect: Changes sensitivity to coordinate differences; p=1 is more robust to outliers in single coordinates than p=2.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: p selection affects sensitivity to feature differences; tuned with metric.
interactions: Interacts with metric choice and scaling.
commonmistakes: Not testing p when domain signals suggest Manhattan-like effects (sparse, per-dimension importance).

hyperparameters.name: metric_params
hyperparameters.purpose: Additional keyword arguments for the metric function (e.g., VI matrix for Mahalanobis).
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Affects accuracy by customizing distance geometry; computational cost increases depending on the metric.
hyperparameters.decreaseeffect: Reverting to standard metrics simplifies execution but loses custom geometry.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Powerful when valid domain covariance is known, but requires careful estimation and computational cost.
commonmistakes: Using estimated covariance from small samples leading to numeric instability.

hyperparameters.name: n_jobs
hyperparameters.purpose: Number of parallel jobs to run for neighbor search and predictions.
hyperparameters.increaseeffect: Improves query throughput up to hardware and parallelism limits; memory usage may increase due to parallel copies.
hyperparameters.tradeoffs: Parallelism reduces query latency for batch workloads but is limited by memory bandwidth.
interactions: Interacts with search algorithm (some indices are not fully parallelizable).
commonmistakes: Setting n_jobs higher than available cores leading to contention; forgetting to profile memory usage when increasing parallelism.

datasetsuitability: Practical for small-to-medium sample sizes (n); for large n, approximate nearest neighbor libraries (ANN) are required.
Struggles on dense/sparse high-dimensional feature spaces where Euclidean distance degrades (curse of dimensionality).
Feature dimensionality should satisfy p << 50 to prevent tree indices from degrading to brute-force search.
Mixed feature types require careful encoding (e.g., target or frequency encoding) as arbitrary categorical encodings distort distance calculations.
scalability: Scales poorly with n and p for exact brute-force search; search cost is CPU and memory bandwidth bound.
Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) libraries (e.g., FAISS, Annoy, HNSW) extend scale to millions of vectors by trading exactness for search speed.
Memory footprint is O(n p) to store the raw dataset, plus index overhead of O(n) to O(n log n).
engineeringconsiderations.parallelization: Horizontal query parallelization is supported via multi-core execution (n_jobs parameter). However, throughput is often bottlenecked by memory bandwidth and distance computation overhead.
engineeringconsiderations.computationalcost: Training is nominal at O(1) or O(n log n) for building trees. Prediction via brute force is O(n p) per query, which is expensive at scale. KD-Tree/Ball-Tree average query time is O(log n) but degrades to O(n) in high dimensions.
engineeringconsiderations.memorybehavior: Memory usage scales linearly with the dataset size O(n p) as all training samples must be stored in memory for query-time distance calculations, along with tree-based index structures.
engineeringconsiderations.inferencecharacteristics: Inference latency is high and CPU-bound due to query-time distance evaluations; batch predictions can amortize vector setup costs but still require individual neighborhood searches.
robustness: Robust to monotonic feature transformations when using rank-based scaling, but highly sensitive to scale differences.
Outlier sensitivity is high when k is small, as predictions can be dominated by nearby noisy samples.
Noisy labels degrade performance; larger neighborhood sizes (k) or distance weighting is required to stabilize predictions.
engineeringconsiderations.sensitivitytooutliers: High sensitivity to feature outliers and noisy samples at small neighborhood sizes (k). Feature outliers directly distort Minkowski distances, while noisy labels within the local neighborhood skew voting/averaging.
engineeringconsiderations.featureengineeringdependency: High dependency: requires domain-specific feature selection and dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA, NCA) to remove irrelevant features, which would otherwise distort distance computations.
engineeringconsiderations.featurescalingrequirement: Mandatory: all features must be scaled to the same range (e.g., via StandardScaler or MinMaxScaler). Otherwise, features with larger magnitudes will dominate distance calculations and dictate neighbor selection.
engineeringconsiderations.classimbalancebehavior: Leaf predictions are naturally biased toward the majority class because majority class samples will dominate local neighborhoods. Mitigated via distance-weighted voting, class-weighted sampling, or adjusting the decision threshold.
commonlimitations: Curse of dimensionality reduces neighbor relevance in high-dimensional spaces.
High inference latency and query cost scaling with dataset size.
High memory consumption to store the entire training dataset.
Extreme sensitivity to feature scaling and irrelevant/noisy features.
engineeringconsiderations.pipelineposition: Positioned as the final estimator in the machine learning pipeline, immediately following imputation, categorical encoding, scaling (StandardScaler), and optional dimensionality reduction (PCA).

comparisons.choose_this_when: Data is small, and you need example-based explanations and local decision behavior.
comparisons.prefer_other_when: You need a compact, fast-to-serve parametric model with well-calibrated probabilities and better performance in high-dimensional sparse spaces.
comparisons.tradeoffs: KNN trades memory and query cost for interpretability; logistic regression trades interpretability of examples for a compact weight vector and speed.

comparisons.choose_this_when: You want neighbor-based similarity and smoothly adjustable locality via k.
comparisons.prefer_other_when: You need a single compact rule set, faster inference per sample, and easier serialization.
comparisons.tradeoffs: KNN requires storing data; trees produce rules and faster tree-traversal inference at similar model size.

comparisons.choose_this_when: You prefer a simple baseline and need very low variance from a single compact model.
comparisons.prefer_other_when: You need ensemble-level accuracy, robustness over noisy data, and stability across folds.
comparisons.tradeoffs: KNN is simple and interpretable by example; RF trades interpretability for reduced variance and typically better accuracy.

comparisons.choose_this_when: Data is small, and interpretability via neighbors is beneficial.
comparisons.prefer_other_when: You need strong margin-based performance, especially with kernels, and better scalability with feature transformations.
comparisons.tradeoffs: KNN retains raw-instance logic and needs storage; SVM provides a compact support-vector representation but can be costly to train.

comparisons.choose_this_when: You want instance-based similarity and non-parametric local decisions.
comparisons.prefer_other_when: Data fits conditional independence assumptions or high-dimensional sparse text where NB is fast and effective.
comparisons.tradeoffs: KNN is flexible but expensive at query time; NB is computationally cheap and robust in specific domains.

comparisons.choose_this_when: Quick baseline by similarity and example explanations favor KNN.
comparisons.prefer_other_when: You prioritize top-tier tabular performance, efficient training with regularization, and scalable deployment.
comparisons.tradeoffs: KNN is simple and interpretable; XGBoost is typically far more accurate but requires training and tuning and produces less-human-readable decision logic.

quickstart.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix

# Example dataframe (replace with real data)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": [25, 45, 35, np.nan, 52, 23, 41, 36],
    "income": [50000, 90000, 65000, 58000, np.nan, 48000, 72000, 61000],
    "city": ["Tokyo", "Osaka", "Tokyo", "Nagoya", "Osaka", "Tokyo", "Nagoya", "Tokyo"],
    "target": [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0],
})

X = df.drop(columns=["target"])
y = df["target"]

num_cols = ["age", "income"]
cat_cols = ["city"]

numeric_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
])

categorical_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
])

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", numeric_pipeline, num_cols),
    ("cat", categorical_pipeline, cat_cols),
])

knn = KNeighborsClassifier()

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("pre", preprocessor),
    ("clf", knn),
])

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

param_grid = {
    "clf__n_neighbors": [3, 5, 7],
    "clf__weights": ["uniform", "distance"],
    "clf__metric": ["minkowski"],
    "clf__p": [1, 2],
    "clf__n_jobs": [-1],
}

search = GridSearchCV(pipeline, param_grid, cv=3, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

best = search.best_estimator_
y_pred = best.predict(X_test)
y_proba = best.predict_proba(X_test) if hasattr(best.named_steps["clf"], "predict_proba") else None

print("Best params:", search.best_params_)
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print("Confusion matrix:\n", confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))
quickstart.explanation: Trains a K-Nearest Neighbors classifier on tabular data using scikit-learn. The pipeline handles missing values, categorical encoding, and feature scaling, which is critical for distance-based estimators. GridSearchCV is used to tune k, metric geometry, and neighborhood voting weights.
quickstart.inputs: Tabular DataFrame with numeric and categorical columns. Targets are discrete class labels (binary or multi-class).
quickstart.outputs: Predicted class labels and corresponding class probability estimates (based on local neighborhood proportions), along with model classification report and confusion matrix.
quickstart.notes: Feature scaling is mandatory because Minkowski distances are scale-sensitive. For large-scale data, consider using approximate nearest neighbor libraries like FAISS or hnswlib instead of scikit-learn's exact search algorithms.
